title: Scenes from World History
description: Ten calm scenes from the past: a copyist in Alexandria, a Silk Road caravan, the carving of Angkor Wat, a Pacific voyage by the stars, the keepers of Timbuktu's manuscripts, an apprentice among the Hanseatic merchants, Japan's first railway, the Athens Games of 1896, a soprano's arrival in New York and an early online debate about history.

lessons.title: The Copyist of Alexandria
lessons.summary: A young copyist arrives at the great Library, learns how its kings collected books and hears a student explain the pronoun.
lessons.text:
In the second century BC, a young man named Ariston sailed to Alexandria to work in its famous Library. Nothing on his quiet Greek island had prepared him for the city that Alexander the Great had founded. The first thing he saw from the deck of his ship, long before he could make out the harbor, was the lighthouse.

The lighthouse stood on the island of Pharos, at the mouth of the harbor, and it was taller than any building Ariston had ever imagined. At night a fire burned at its summit, and sailors could see it far out at sea. To Ariston it seemed a promise: here was a city that kept a light burning for strangers.

The Library's shelves held tens of thousands of scrolls, and its kings were perpetual collectors, never satisfied with what they had. Ships that entered the harbor were searched for books; the books were copied, and the owners, it was said, received the copies while the originals stayed in the Library. Another story concerned Athens, which had lent the king its official copies of the great tragedies. The loan was conditional: he had to leave a large deposit and return the scrolls. The king accepted the conditional loan, then kept the originals, sent back new copies and let Athens keep the deposit. Ariston found the story humorous, although he suspected that the Athenians had not found it humorous at all.

He was given work under a scholar who was preparing a new edition of Homer. The scholar was a firm proponent of careful comparison: before deciding what Homer had really written, one had to read a line in every available copy. Other scholars preferred to trust their own taste, and whenever a proponent of one method met a proponent of the other, a long debate would ensue. Ariston learned to listen without taking sides and to wait for whatever ensued.

What interested him most, however, was grammar. An older student was dividing the Greek language into its parts, and he explained his ideas over dinner. There was the noun, which names a thing, and the verb, which says what it does. Then there was the pronoun, a word that stands in place of a noun. "When you say 'he' instead of 'Achilles'," the student said, "you are using a pronoun." Ariston had used pronouns all his life without knowing that they had a name, and the discovery felt like being handed the key to a house he already lived in.

Copying was a perpetual struggle against tired eyes and dry pens, but the conversations were informative. Walking along the harbor as the lighthouse began to shine, Ariston felt that he had come to the right place: a city where even a word as small as "he" was worth an informative evening of talk.

Questions:
What was the first thing Ariston saw as he sailed toward Alexandria?
He saw the lighthouse on the island of Pharos.
On what condition did Athens lend its copies of the tragedies?
The loan was conditional: the king had to leave a large deposit and return the scrolls.
What happened whenever scholars with different methods met?
A long debate would ensue, and Ariston learned to listen without taking sides.
What is a pronoun, according to the older student?
A pronoun is a word that stands in place of a noun, such as "he" instead of "Achilles."

lessons.title: A Caravan Leaves Samarkand
lessons.summary: A Sogdian merchant leads a caravan of camels and mules east from Samarkand along the Silk Road.
lessons.text:
Early in the eighth century, when Samarkand was one of the richest cities on the Silk Road, a merchant named Farnak prepared to lead a caravan east toward China. The Sogdians, Farnak's people, were the great traders of the route. They seldom traveled the whole way themselves; they carried goods from one city to the next, and their families had settled in trading towns all the way to China. Thanks to this patient network, Sogdian merchants had prospered for generations, and Farnak meant to prosper too.

In a dusty yard outside the city walls, the caravan was assembled. There were camels, and there were mules, which Farnak valued for the mountain passes where camels struggled. A mule is the child of a horse and a donkey, and it has the strength of the first and the stubborn temper of the second. The drivers spent the morning hitching the mules together in long lines, and every time a mule refused to be hitched, the whole yard stopped to watch the argument.

Going east, Farnak carried silver vessels, colored glass and small bottles of perfume; coming back, he hoped to carry silk. Every bale was wrapped in felt and oiled leather, which made it almost waterproof, because a single storm could ruin a fortune in cloth. Farnak checked each waterproof cover himself.

They set out at dawn, with freshly baked bread in their bags. Farnak always said that a journey should begin with freshly baked bread, because nothing on the road would taste as good. They passed orchards and fields, and once, at the edge of the dry plains, they met a small tortoise crossing the track at its own pace. The drivers stopped the camels to let it pass. Farnak said that the tortoise was the wisest of all who used the road: it carried its house on its back and never hurried.

Later the land grew harder. In the mountains, cold winds buffeted the caravan for days, pushing at the loads and stinging the faces of the men. The mules, steady and sure-footed, earned their place on the narrow paths. Farnak had heard older merchants speak of the brutality of the deserts further east, where the sun burned by day and the cold bit by night, and as the wind buffeted him, he understood that the brutality of the land was part of the price of silk.

Each evening they stopped at an inn built around a courtyard, where merchants from many countries slept under one roof. Then the men sat around a fire and ate a stew of lamb and onions, cooked slowly in a great iron pot. After a day in the wind, the stew tasted like a feast.

The wind might buffet them, but the caravan would move on, as caravans had for centuries, from one fire and one bowl of stew to the next.

Questions:
Why did Farnak value mules?
He valued them for the mountain passes, where camels struggled.
How did the merchants protect the bales of cloth?
Every bale was wrapped in felt and oiled leather, which made it almost waterproof.
Why did Farnak call the tortoise the wisest of all who used the road?
He said it carried its house on its back and never hurried.
What did the men eat in the evenings?
They ate a stew of lamb and onions, cooked slowly in a great iron pot.

lessons.title: The Stone Carver of Angkor
lessons.summary: A young carver works on the sandstone walls of Angkor Wat while the great temple slowly rises.
lessons.text:
Around the year 1120, the Khmer king Suryavarman the Second ordered the building of a temple that would become the largest religious monument in the world. It was dedicated to the god Vishnu, and today we call it Angkor Wat. A young man named Sok came to work there as a stone cutter when he was sixteen. The temple would go on rising for most of his life.

The temple was made of sandstone. The stone came from quarries in the hills about twenty-five miles away, and most historians believe that it traveled along canals and rivers on rafts. A single block could weigh 1,500 kilograms, and there were millions of blocks. Sok loved to watch the workers lift them into place with ropes and wooden frames, as if 1,500 kilograms were a basket of rice. The sandstone was soft enough to cut with an iron tool, which is why the builders chose it.

Sok's master worked on the long galleries around the temple's center. Their walls were covered with carvings, and one of them was a depiction of an old story: gods and demons pulling on a great snake to stir the ocean and win the drink of eternal life. The depiction stretched for about fifty yards. Sok spent a whole year on a small part of it, cutting the scales of the snake and the fingers of the gods.

Then he was given the doorways. Beside each doorway stood carved female figures, goddesses and heavenly dancers with tall crowns and jewels, and no two of them were alike. Sok carved one of them with a care he would remember all his life. His master, who praised almost nothing, called the work exquisite, and Sok walked home that night as if he were floating. Years later, visitors would still call those dancers exquisite.

In the mornings, the priests chanted in the temple, and Sok often heard the sacred word om, long and low, rising from the inner courts. The priests said that om was the sound from which the world had come. Sok did not fully understand this, but he liked to work with om in his ears.

As the years passed, the shape of the whole temple became clear. Its main facade faced west, toward the setting sun, and was reflected in the wide water that surrounded the temple. Above the facade rose five towers whose shape was reminiscent of lotus buds about to open. They were also meant to be reminiscent of something greater: the holy mountain where the gods live. The forest made a dark green backdrop behind them, and at sunset the towers glowed against that backdrop like coals.

Sok spent his life on a few doorways and a few yards of wall. Yet when he stood before the western facade at sunset, he felt that every one of his small marks belonged to the whole.

Questions:
Why did the builders choose sandstone?
The sandstone was soft enough to cut with an iron tool.
How much could a single block weigh?
A single block could weigh 1,500 kilograms.
What did the long depiction on the gallery wall show?
It showed gods and demons pulling on a great snake to stir the ocean and win the drink of eternal life.
What was the shape of the towers reminiscent of?
It was reminiscent of lotus buds about to open, and of the holy mountain where the gods live.

lessons.title: Sailing Without Instruments
lessons.summary: In 1976 a master sailor guides a traditional canoe from Hawaii to Tahiti using only the stars, the waves and the birds.
lessons.text:
For a long time, the achievement of the first people to settle the islands of the Pacific was misunderstood. They had found tiny islands scattered across the largest ocean on Earth, and they had done it in canoes, without maps or instruments. As late as 1956, one theorist argued that the islands had been settled by accident, by canoes that drifted off course and happened to reach land. His book was widely read, and many people came to believe, falsely, that the great voyages had been a matter of luck.

In 1976, a group of Hawaiians decided to test the question at sea. They had built a large double canoe, the Hōkūleʻa, in the style of the old canoes, and they planned to sail it from Hawaii to Tahiti, about 2,500 miles, without a compass or a map. They asked Mau Piailug, a master sailor from Satawal, a small island in Micronesia, to guide them, because he was one of the last people who still knew the old methods.

Mau read the ocean the way a scholar reads a book. At night he steered by the stars, watching where each one rose and set on the horizon. By day he watched the swells, the long waves that travel for thousands of miles. The ocean is in constant flux, and the swells change with the wind and the season, so his methods had to be adaptive: when clouds hid the stars, he relied on the waves, and when the waves grew confused, he waited for the stars. To the crew, his choices often seemed intuitive, almost magical. But what looked intuitive was knowledge so deep that he no longer needed to explain it.

Mau seemed to feel the sea through his body. When two swells met beneath the canoe, the crew said, the hulls would vibrate in a particular way, and from the way they vibrated he could tell where the waves were coming from. Even while he slept, the canoe rocked on the swells like a cradle, and the crew noticed that he woke whenever the rhythm of that cradle changed.

Near the end of the voyage, Mau watched for birds. Certain sea birds fly out from land in the morning to fish and return in the evening, so their flight points toward islands that are still unseen. For days Tahiti remained unseen beyond the horizon. Then the birds came, and the crew followed them.

The canoe reached Tahiti about a month after leaving Hawaii, and thousands of people came to the shore to greet it. The voyage showed that the old methods worked and that the theorist had been wrong: the ancient voyages had been falsely described as lucky accidents. Mau went on to teach his adaptive methods to many younger sailors, who still learn to read an ocean in flux. The skill of the old Pacific sailors, misunderstood for centuries, is still one of the most underrated achievements in human history, though it is far less underrated than it was in 1956.

Questions:
What did one theorist argue in 1956?
He argued that the islands had been settled by accident.
Why did Mau's methods have to be adaptive?
The ocean is in constant flux, and the swells change with the wind and the season.
How could Mau feel the waves through his body?
When two swells met beneath the canoe, the hulls would vibrate in a particular way.
How did the birds help the crew find Tahiti?
Their flight from land and back points toward unseen islands.

lessons.title: The Manuscript Doctor
lessons.summary: In Bamako, a woman who repairs old books cares for the manuscripts of Timbuktu.
lessons.text:
Every morning at eight, Aminata unlocks a cool, quiet room in Bamako, the capital of Mali, puts her handbag on the shelf by the door and pulls on a pair of cotton gloves. She repairs old books for a living. Her patients, as she likes to call them, are manuscripts from Timbuktu.

Timbuktu, on the edge of the Sahara near the Niger River, grew rich on trade five hundred years ago and became a famous center of learning. Books were copied, bought and sold, and families built private libraries that they passed down from parent to child. Hundreds of thousands of these manuscripts survive, most of them written in Arabic, on law, medicine, poetry, mathematics and the stars.

For centuries, each family would entrust its library to one member of every generation, who would guard it and entrust it in turn to the next. In 2012, during a period of unrest in the north of the country, librarians and families quietly moved most of the manuscripts south to Bamako, packed in metal trunks. Since the unrest, many of them have stayed in Bamako, far from the dry air of the desert.

That is the problem Aminata faces. Bamako is much damper than Timbuktu, and in damp air old paper can deteriorate quickly. Mold grows, insects arrive and ink fades; a page left alone for a few years can deteriorate beyond repair. In the past, collections were sometimes treated with strong chemicals against insects, but Aminata avoids them because of their toxicity, both for the paper and for the people who handle it. Instead, she seals damaged books in closed boxes until the insects die, a slower method with no toxicity at all.

Arthritis has made her own fingers stiff, especially in the rainy season, and every morning she warms them on a cup of tea before she picks up her brush. Despite the arthritis, her hands are steady once she begins.

Today's patient is a book on medicine. Its first pages are missing, so its author remains unidentified, like the authors of many manuscripts in the collection. The unidentified scholar describes plants and warns that one of them is a narcotic: in small amounts it eases pain, but in large amounts it brings a sleep from which some never wake. Aminata thinks that the warning about the narcotic would satisfy any modern doctor.

The next book on her table is about the stars. In the past, astronomy and astrology were not clearly separated, and the same scholar who calculated the times of prayer might also write about astrology, the belief that the stars shape human lives.

In the corner, a small router blinks green. Next door, a team photographs every page so that scholars anywhere can read the manuscripts online. When a storm cuts the power and the router goes dark, they drink tea and wait.

At five, Aminata takes off her gloves, picks up her handbag and turns off the light.

Questions:
Why were the manuscripts moved to Bamako?
During a period of unrest in 2012, librarians and families moved them south.
Why can the manuscripts deteriorate in Bamako?
Bamako is much damper than Timbuktu, and in damp air old paper can deteriorate quickly.
Why does Aminata avoid strong chemicals?
She avoids them because of their toxicity.
What does the unidentified author say about one of the plants?
The author warns that it is a narcotic that eases pain in small amounts but is dangerous in large amounts.

lessons.title: An Apprentice at Bergen
lessons.summary: A boy from Lübeck learns the stockfish trade among the Hanseatic merchants of Bergen.
lessons.text:
In the middle of the fifteenth century, a boy of thirteen named Hinrik left Lübeck on a merchant ship bound for Bergen, on the west coast of Norway. Lübeck led the Hansa, a league of trading towns along the northern seas, and in Bergen the Hansa had one of its great trading houses, where German merchants lived and worked beside the harbor. Hinrik was to spend ten years there as an apprentice.

The trade at Bergen was built on stockfish: cod dried in the cold wind of northern Norway until it was as hard as wood. It kept for years. In return the merchants brought grain, which Norway could not grow in large amounts.

Hinrik's new life was spartan. He slept in a narrow wooden bed in a building that was never heated, because fire was the greatest danger in a town made of wood. The only warm places were the shared halls behind the houses, where the men ate their meals and spent the winter evenings. Hinrik soon decided that a spartan life was easier on a full stomach.

Every man in the trading house had to remain single, and the apprentices had little time to socialize with the people of the town. They socialized among themselves instead, in the warm halls. It rained in Bergen more often than Hinrik had thought possible, and the wooden paths along the water were always slippery. On his first day he dropped a bundle of fish on the slippery boards, and the older boys laughed at him for a week.

His master taught him to judge fish by its look and smell, and to check every set of scales and every weight. "An honest weight is a merchant's good name," he said. He showed Hinrik an old weight with a rusty iron ring and explained that a rusty weight must be tested, because rust can change it. The merchants' own court punished fraudulent weights severely. In Hinrik's second year, a merchant from another house was indicted for using a fraudulent weight; when the court found him guilty, he paid a heavy fine and lost the trust of the other merchants, which was worse. Hinrik never forgot the man who was indicted that spring.

His master also told him about the power of the Hansa. Long ago, he said, after a dispute with the king of Norway, the Hansa towns had stopped all grain ships from reaching the country. The obstruction lasted until Norway agreed to give the merchants new privileges. The Norwegians called the obstruction blackmail; the merchants called it business. Hinrik noticed that his master did not smile when he said the word blackmail.

By the time he was twenty-three, Hinrik's competence was beyond question, and his master trusted that competence completely. He returned to Lübeck as a merchant. The trading house at Bergen lasted for about three more centuries before its slow dissolution. The dissolution of the Hansa itself was just as slow: it simply faded, town by town.

Questions:
Why was Hinrik's building never heated?
Fire was the greatest danger in a town made of wood.
Why were the wooden paths always slippery?
It rained in Bergen very often.
What happened to the merchant who used a fraudulent weight?
He was indicted, found guilty, paid a heavy fine and lost the trust of the other merchants.
What did the Norwegians call the obstruction of grain ships?
They called it blackmail.

lessons.title: The First Train in Japan
lessons.summary: A visitor to Tokyo learns from an old railway man how Japan's first line opened in 1872.
lessons.text:
I arrived in Tokyo on a gray October morning and took the airport bus into the city. In Japan this bus is called a limousine, a word that made me picture a long black car with a driver in white gloves. The real limousine was a large, quiet bus that left exactly on time, and it carried me to the business district that now stands where Tokyo's first railway station once stood.

The old station, Shimbashi, has been rebuilt on its original site as a small stone museum. At the door, a white-haired guide bowed and said, "Welcome, mister." He had worked on the railways for forty years, and he still remembered his first payday. "I spent half of my wages on a model train," he told me, laughing. "My mother said it was a strange way to celebrate payday."

He showed me old photographs and maps and told me the story. In 1854 Japan had begun to open its ports to the world after more than two centuries of isolation, and by 1872 its new Meiji government wanted to learn quickly from the West. Yokohama, about eighteen miles from Tokyo, was the main port for foreign trade, the home of foreign merchants and of the consulates of many countries. The two cities had been joined by a telegraph line since 1869, and a telegram could cross the distance in moments. But a telegram could not carry people or goods, so the government decided to build a railway, with engineers from Britain to help.

The line opened on 14 October 1872. The emperor himself rode the train from Shimbashi to Yokohama and back, together with ministers and foreign diplomats, among them officials from the consulates of Yokohama. The journey took less than an hour, a trip that had once taken most of a day. The guide described it so well that the scene felt cinematic: the black engine, the flags, the crowds along the tracks, and the emperor stepping down at the end of the line. I said that it sounded like a cinematic opening, and he agreed that it was the opening of a new age.

He was honest about the downsides. Tickets were expensive at first, and only the rich could ride often. Another downside was the smoke. Some people worried that the engines would pollute the air and that sparks would set their roofs on fire. "Today our trains are electric," the guide said, "so they pollute far less than those first engines did."

From 1872 onwards, railways spread across Japan, and by 1889 a line ran all the way from Tokyo to Kobe. From that day onwards, the guide said, the country never moved at the old speed again.

When I left, he bowed once more. "Come back soon, mister," he said. I walked out into the noise of modern Tokyo, where trains pass every few minutes, and thought of that first slow journey to the sea.

Questions:
Why did the visitor find the word limousine surprising?
It made the visitor picture a long black car, but the real limousine was a large, quiet bus.
How did the guide spend his first payday?
He spent half of his wages on a model train.
Why was a telegram not enough to connect Tokyo and Yokohama?
A telegram could not carry people or goods.
What were two downsides of the first railway?
Tickets were expensive, and some people worried that the smoke would pollute the air.

lessons.title: The Games Return to Athens
lessons.summary: A writer visits the marble stadium of Athens and tells the story of the first modern Olympic Games in 1896.
lessons.text:
The marble stadium in the center of Athens is quiet on a winter morning. I sat on one of its white benches with the small guide booklet I had bought at the gate, and I tried to imagine the noise of April 1896, when this stadium held the first modern Olympic Games.

The idea had come from Pierre de Coubertin, a French educator who believed that sport could build character and bring nations together. He wanted to revive the games of ancient Greece. The stadium itself was an ancient one, rebuilt in white marble for the occasion, and according to my booklet, it held tens of thousands of people on the busiest days.

By modern standards the Games were tiny. About 240 athletes came from 14 countries, all of them men. Yet the Games of 1896 were the embryo of something much larger. Like any embryo, they already held the shape of what was to come: the opening ceremony, the national flags, the medals and the crowds.

The most famous race was the marathon, a new event inspired by an old story about a messenger who ran from Marathon to Athens. The runners covered about twenty-five miles of dusty road in the heat. Several of them gave up in agony, and those who continued ran through the agony of the last miles on courage alone. The winner was a Greek water carrier named Spyridon Louis. As he entered the stadium, two Greek princes ran beside him to the finish, and the crowd cheered as if the whole nation had won.

There is a popular story about Louis. During the race, it is said, he stopped at a village tavern and drank a glass of wine before running on. Whether the story is factual, no one can say for certain. But people have repeated the tale of the tavern for more than a century, perhaps because it makes a great champion seem so human. The time he ran, close to three hours, is factual and well recorded.

News of the Games traveled fast. Newspapers, printed on rotary presses that could turn out thousands of copies an hour, carried the results across Europe and America within days. In a sense, the rotary press gave the Olympic idea an audience far larger than any stadium.

It has become a cliché to say that the important thing in the Games is not winning but taking part. Coubertin made the idea famous in 1908, after hearing it in a sermon, and like every cliché it has lost some of its force through constant use. The history of the Games has not always been simple, either. South Africa, for example, was kept out of the Games from 1964 to 1988 because of apartheid, the system that separated people by race. As apartheid was coming to an end, the country returned to the Games in 1992.

When I left, the stadium was still quiet, but I could almost hear the crowd of 1896.

Questions:
Why were the Games of 1896 called an embryo?
They already held the shape of what was to come, like any embryo.
What happened to several of the marathon runners?
Several of them gave up in agony.
What popular story is told about Spyridon Louis?
It is said that he stopped at a village tavern and drank a glass of wine before running on.
Why was South Africa kept out of the Games from 1964 to 1988?
It was kept out because of apartheid, the system that separated people by race.

lessons.title: The Swedish Soprano in New York
lessons.summary: In 1850 the singer Jenny Lind arrives in New York and gives her first American concert.
lessons.text:
On the first day of September 1850, a ship from England came into New York harbor, and tens of thousands of people were waiting at the pier. They had come to see a woman most of them had never heard sing: Jenny Lind, a soprano from Stockholm who was already the most admired singer in Europe.

Her tour was the work of Barnum, a famous entertainer who owned a museum of curiosities. Barnum had offered Lind an enormous sum for a long series of concerts, and before she arrived he filled the newspapers with stories about her talent, her kindness and her simple life. By the time her ship docked, the city was in love with a voice it had never heard.

The attention never stopped. Crowds gathered outside her hotel day and night, and one night a band played under her windows at midnight. Lind was polite to everyone, but she found the constant noise irritating, and there were days when the endless crowds seemed enough to madden her. Her rooms were filled with flowers sent by fans, and the heavy fragrance of so many flowers was almost too much. She sometimes opened the windows to let out the fragrance and let in the cool night air, but then the irritating noise came in with it.

Shops, meanwhile, discovered that her name could sell anything. There was a rapid proliferation of Jenny Lind gloves, Jenny Lind hats, Jenny Lind pianos and even Jenny Lind beds; a style of children's bed still carries her name today. Newspaper writers who disliked Barnum's methods complained that the proliferation of her name was enough to madden any serious lover of music.

Her first concert took place on 11 September at Castle Garden, a large hall at the southern tip of Manhattan. Tickets were sold at auction, and the first one went for 225 dollars, a fortune at the time. Thousands of attendees filled the hall, and when she stepped onto the stage, the attendees fell silent.

Her first song was an aria from an Italian opera, a slow and difficult piece that showed the full range of her voice. When the aria ended, the hall shook with applause. Later in the evening she sang simpler songs, including a Swedish song from the mountains. On other evenings of the tour she often added the old ballad "Home, Sweet Home." For many listeners, a simple ballad was the most moving moment of a concert, because it showed that her voice did not need difficult music to touch the heart.

After her first concerts, Lind gave her share of the earnings to the charities of New York. She went on to sing across the country, and when she finally sailed home, people in America spoke of her for years as the kind soprano who had come to them across the sea.

Questions:
Why were tens of thousands of people waiting at the pier?
They had come to see Jenny Lind, a soprano from Stockholm.
Why did Lind sometimes open the windows of her rooms?
She opened them to let out the heavy fragrance of the flowers and let in the cool night air.
What did the proliferation of her name lead to in the shops?
There were Jenny Lind gloves, hats, pianos and even beds.
What was her first song at the concert?
It was an aria from an Italian opera that showed the full range of her voice.

lessons.title: Arguing About Alexandria Online
lessons.summary: A retired teacher remembers the early internet newsgroup where she and other history lovers argued about the Library of Alexandria.
lessons.text:
In 1994, when I was teaching history at a high school in Ohio, my brother set up a computer in my kitchen and showed me something called a newsgroup. A newsgroup, he explained, was a public discussion board on the early internet: anyone could post a message on a subject, and anyone could answer. There were thousands of newsgroups, and one of them was about ancient history. I joined it that night, sitting at the kitchen table with a slice of raspberry pie, and I stayed for six years.

The connection was slow, and we paid for it by the hour, so in the first months a surprising part of my paycheck went to the telephone company. My husband said that I was spending my paycheck on arguments with strangers, and he was not entirely wrong. The newsgroup was addictive. I would sit down after dinner to read one message and look up to find that it was midnight, the raspberry pie forgotten beside the keyboard. Few things in my life have been as addictive as a good argument about the past.

Our favorite subject was the Library of Alexandria, and especially the question of how it was lost. Every few weeks, someone new would arrive with a simple, dramatic story: the Library had been destroyed in a single great fire on a single terrible day. The regular members would explain, with patience, that the truth was slower and sadder. The evidence suggests that the Library declined over several centuries, as money and support ran out and scholars left, and that the famous single fire is closer to legend than to history.

The newsgroup also attracted pseudo-history: claims that Atlantis had been real, or that the pyramids had been built by visitors from another world. Most people who posted such pseudo-history were simply having fun, but a few seemed to live in a kind of delusion that no evidence could reach. We learned to answer once, kindly, and then let the delusion rest.

The best member of the group was a biker from Indiana named Gus, who repaired motorcycles for a living and read Greek history in the evenings. He knew more about Alexandria than most professors, and we called him "the biker" with affection. Once, as a joke, he worked out a coefficient of correlation, a number that shows how closely two things go together, between the length of our messages and how often they were correct. The coefficient was negative: the longer the message, the more likely it was to be wrong.

Whenever someone repeated the myth of the single fire, Gus would post a short riff on it, inventing ever sillier causes, such as a cat knocking over a lamp. Every riff ended with the same line: "Check your sources."

Today my grandson argues about crypto with the same excitement that we once brought to Alexandria, and his friends answer him about crypto until midnight. I listen and smile. The subjects change, but people still love to argue late at night.

Questions:
What was a newsgroup?
It was a public discussion board on the early internet.
Why did part of the writer's paycheck go to the telephone company?
The connection was paid for by the hour.
What did the regular members believe about how the Library was lost?
They believed it declined slowly, over several centuries.
What did the biker's coefficient show?
It was negative: the longer the message, the more likely it was to be wrong.
